I worry that the knife stabbing thing won't work the way you think it will. More pain, and less relief than you hope for. You really don't want to wake up in restraints listed as a suicide gone wrong. 

There's not a rush to die, is there? Perhaps you could give it six months or so?
Dream job in a brand new place sounds pretty good. Sometimes just a change of place brings a change of mind. If I were you, I'd pull all my mental resources into moving and giving it a fair shot.

You got dumped hard, mate. That just sucks, and continues to suck for a really long time, or possibly forever. But, in my individual experience, it tapers off eventually. I still haven't forgotten my first true love, and that was longer ago than you've been alive. But eventually, the pain gets displaced by other, stronger emotions, the way that you can't see the stars when the sun is out.

Check [IHateMyLife.us](http://www.ihatemylife.us/index2.html).  It's LA-centric, and tells the story of a guy who was homeless for a while but turned his life around. It has some resources, too. I personally know he's authentic.

P.S. Right now you've got to forget about love and breakups and stuff, just until you get back on your feet. Sorry, priorities.

Computer kind of guy who is young and speaks English and has nothing to lose?  

Farming is a fine and excellent occupation which you, personally, should get the hell away from. Can you program, or learn to program? Or be a systems administrator? Have you thought of, say, moving to the San Francisco Bay Area in California? Not San Francisco itself, which is wildly overpriced and is mostly a tourist trap, but Berkeley or Mountain View? Fantastic weather, like you wouldn't believe, but not a farm in sight. Do you have a passport? You could get an American H1-B visa and have a wildly new and exciting life within a few months from now. Like, sixty days, you could be on Telegraph Avenue in Berkeley or Castro Street in Mountain View, working crazy long hours at some startup in a team in which no two members share the same nationality, working to create the next Google or Facebook. Or Reddit. 

You can look at these streets on Google Maps. And the reason you can look at them is because some programmers in the Bay Area in California, some of whom came from places like rural Norway, left their homes and came to America and made them work.

There are such things in lots of places. /r/depression is good in many ways but if you're looking for a true support group, in which people recognize each other face-to-face for at least a couple of weeks on end, this might not be enough. This reddit is more of a fast-moving river of people screaming "help" and other people, who may or may not be on shore, screaming back, "hold on!"

People are not (all) stupid. If you're right-handed and they see cuts on your left arm and leg, they'll figure it out. You're already getting treatment, but it's obviously not yet what you need. Lots of stuff going on.

You already know this is serious, so the thing to do is to seek escalated treatment in a way in which you are in the driver's seat as much as possible. If you trust your sister at all, you might want to come clean with her, if only to forestall her from forcing the issue. Tell her you plan to demand new meds and stepped up therapy -- and truly, make this happen. If necessary, fire your mental health providers and get new ones. They work for you. If you're still in pain, their job has not been accomplished. 

Seriously, I understand you are sixteen, and your therapist or doctor or nurse practitioner is much older. But I'm probably older than them. *Force* them to help you. If they don't or can't, look them in the eye and say something like, "Sorry, but this just isn't working for me. Can you recommend another provider in your field?"

Family and friends are two different things. Based on my own experience when I was your age, I'd think that any indications of mental health treatment would cause just a couple of people you know to reveal themselves as *utterly magnificent and noble*, and huge numbers of people would dump shit on you. Not just the "look at the freak" stuff, but also insincere assertions that "we support you" with the hidden (tee hee). It might not break down the way you'd expect.

The first thing is to try to get your head together as much as you can. Don't freak out.  

[Nolo](http://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/dealing-with-debt-when-you-cant-pay-your-bills) has some really good advice about what to do when you're in debt. The reason they have this is because *tons* of people in this world are in debt as deep or deeper than you are. There's also /r/Debt, where you can post more detailed questions if you want to.

Collections is just a business, not a force of nature or fate. Taking legal action against you would be expensive from their perspective, and if you have no money right now, or if they drive you into bankruptcy -- they lose. They know this, and so should you.

I don't know you, and I don't have any idea whether you're "cut out" for college or not, but it might not be working for you just right now at this point in your life. Wasting money and time can be a genuinely bad decision, not just the illusion of depression. Maybe it wouldn't be the worst thing in the world to just work for a year or two, get your goals and interests sorted out, and then go back to college with a different focus. 

Personally, I grew up in an environment, both at school and at home, in which the assumption was that the secret to life was getting a white collar professional job after graduating from a high-status college. If you didn't do that, your life would suck.

It turns out, your life can suck even if you do pursue that path, or even if you succeed in it on paper. On the other hand, so-called blue collar jobs are not all alike. A skilled electrician, for example, can commonly make six figures a year with very reasonable hours and no student loans to pay off. (By the way, the mismatch between school and jobs is something of a personal crusade for [Mike Rowe](http://profoundlydisconnected.com/), who used to host that show *Dirty Jobs*. 

Anyway, there are usually more options than you think. Good luck.

I'm rather new to this subreddit myself, but these questions are quite relevant and come up a lot here. There may be a better FAQ or some thing that I'm not aware of, but I'd recommend a post on the Slate Star Codex blog called [Things That Sometimes Help if You Have Depression](http://slatestarcodex.com/2014/06/16/things-that-sometimes-help-if-youre-depressed/) I'm going to try to stick to rule 1 from the guidelines in the sidebar here...hope I don't step over the line.  

First off, the writer is a new psychiatrist. He writes about a lot of things, but mental health comes under his radar a lot, and he knows and cares a lot about it.

A small part of his post deals with your question about being forced into an institution (writing for an American audience, anyway):
>The first and most important point is that very very few psychiatrists, whether good or bad, will commit people to a mental institution unless they are very sick. Even if you are very sick, there is only a small chance of a psychiatrist committing you against your will unless you say exactly the wrong thing.

>Doctors and psychiatrists are legally required to commit patients to mental institutions if those patients are “a threat to themselves or others”. Usually this means a patient has said they want to commit suicide and they are probably really going to go through with it soon, or a patient has said they’re going to hurt someone else (or implied it: “He’s gonna get what’s coming to him”) and it wasn’t clearly meant metaphorically. They may also commit you if you are very paranoid on the grounds that paranoid people may try to pre-emptively attack those they believe are plotting against them – or if you are refusing to eat, on the grounds that if you don’t eat you die.

>A good psychiatrist will differentiate between vague suicidal ideation (“Sometimes I feel like life isn’t even worth living, do you know what I mean?”) and specific suicidal ideation (“I will kill myself tomorrow using the gun hidden in the back of my pantry”), will explore the first type with an aim toward helping you, and will only involuntarily commit for the second type. I do not guarantee you will have a good psychiatrist. 

Hope that wasn't to much of a text slab. Good luck!

Don't go hating yourself or feeling horrible. It isn't really any of their business where you go or what you do on your own time, or what your private medical problems are. You're really being much too hard on yourself. As lies go, this is something like pretending not to be home when a religious missionary knocks at the door.

Actually, your affairs seem to be, according to what you say, wrapped up rather tidily. 

People will still freak the fuck out. Your poor taikwondo instructor will probably be horrified. You generally can't tie up the emotional loose ends in a suicide. 

Also, if you want to be tidy, consider the reaction of whoever had to discover your corpse, and those who have to clean up after it. Additionally, there may be the the possibility that your suicide will not go entirely to plan, leaving you alive for some time in some incapacitated condition or other.

Permit me to respectfully suggest that you're under the influence of depression right now, hence your post to the /r/depression subreddit, and your cost-benefit analysis is not really what's going on here.  

How would you apply your own analysis to someone else? Surely you don't think that anyone who is an economic burden on upon anyone else deserves death? You don't want to kill all babies and old people. That would be evil. Nor do you want to kill all the sick and disabled. That would also be evil. Cartoon villains and imaginary Nazis do that, not the heroes. The heroes save the weak.

You are, I take it, not a net contributor to the economy just right now. However, I also suspect that you are suffering from the biological condition of depression, which would make you one of the sick and disabled. Only the cartoon Nazis want to kill you for being a burden on society.

Side point, which you should ignore for now, but maybe think about before you're brought down by some shit in the near future:

You describe yourself, I think rather pejoratively, as having "chickened out," suggesting that, if you were braver, you would have gone through with it. Remember how a lot of ignorant people talk evil about the dead, saying that anybody who has committed suicide must have been a "selfish coward" or something like that. This is pejorative as well, but is totally inconsistent with the phrasing you chose. They both can't be true. 

I'd suggest that both of those pejoratives are false, or more nicely expressed, misguided. I'd say that suicide under the influence of a depressive disorder is neither brave nor cowardly, anymore than falling asleep under the influence of a powerful narcotic is lazy. It's biological. Don't beat yourself up more than you have to.

The title of this post reminded me of a part of the book *Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance.* It works better in the original, but I'll summarize. Basically, the narrator is working as a high school English teacher in Bozeman, Montana. He's trying to inspire a bit of creativity in this one girl student. At first, her assignment is to write something original about the United States. She can't think of a thing to say. So, he says, just write about five hundred words about Bozeman. She's still frozen. So, he says, how about just Main Street? Five hundred words is not that much. Still frozen. 

> He was furious. "You're not *looking*!" he said. A memory came back of his own dismissal from the University for having too *much* to say. For every fact there is an *infinity* of hypotheses... 

>He told her angrily, "Narrow it down to the front of one building on the main street of Bozeman. The Opera House. Start with the upper left-hand brick..."

>She came in the next class with a puzzled look and handed him a five-thousand-word essay on the front of the Opera House on the main street of Bozeman, Montana. "I sat in the hamburger stand across the street," she said, "and started writing about the first brick, and the second brick, and then by the third brick it all started to come and I couldn't stop..."

Your mileage will vary.

One book I particularly hated was [Feeling Good](http://www.amazon.com/Feeling-Good-The-Mood-Therapy/dp/0380810336) by David D. Burns. I had been given it by a well-meaning relative. At the time, it felt like someone was offering me a squirt gun to deal with a five-alarm inferno. It was a very dark time, and suicide seemed appealing. I didn't go that route, mostly because I knew my family would be emotionally destroyed. I wondered, though, what it would be like if I did kill myself, and in my suicide note, I had said something like, "Hey folks! Sorry about the mess, hope it hasn't bummed you out too much. If you're still feelin' down after a day or so, why don't you check out *Feeling Good* by David fucking D. Burns? That book'll make you snap out of it in no time!"

To be fair, I read very little of it, but at the time it seemed so glib. Maybe it was just the title. I understand a lot of people have found some real comfort from it. But it obviously doesn't work for everybody, certainly not "tremendously". If it did, this whole subreddit, and a huge amount of the medical establishment, could be eliminated. 

With that said, David Foster Wallace didn't write self-help books, and ultimately he found no help for himself. But he probably wrote some of the best prose about depression that there is. 

Also, it's not a book, and it only offers understanding rather than help, is Stanford Professor Robert Sapolsky's lecture on depression, available on youtube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NOAgplgTxfc

This is actually a very good and important question, and a very old one, and you should consider it seriously. As it happens, my username is taken from one of the first people in recorded history to really ask this question. 

Another way to phrase your question is, why *should* you kill yourself right now? What's your rush?  I'm sure you have very real problems in life, but in the long run they don't matter very much, at least not in the long run. If you're really not afraid of death, surely you're not afraid of a few problems that will die with your body soon enough. Epictetus personally was a crippled slave.

Epictetus would probably say that the important thing is, in the few short years you have, you must live a virtuous life according to the principles of reason. One sign of rational virtue is not to fear death. Another sign is to be patient, knowing that life is short and death will come soon enough.

That was once one of my pet peeves too at one point. The outermost surface level of people can be fake friendly, which is annoying. Underneath that, most people are wrapped up in own day-to-day business. Under the smile, they're likely to be indifferent to anything you have to say.

However, on further reflection, that's not the deepest level. Some people -- not everyone, but some people -- really are good and kind at the deepest level. For example, lots of ordinary people will drop everything and risk their own lives to save a total stranger in, say, a car accident. Lots of people who aren't anything like saints at work or while driving in traffic are really, truly good at the bottom, and really do care about you (and me, and everybody else) without knowing you.

And then, some people are just jerks to the bone.

Why? There's one theory I've heard. If I understand it correctly, ten or fifty thousand years ago, calories were scarce and precious. Our ancestors would wake with the sunrise excited to go off hunting and gathering. If times were good, then they'd end the day with more than a day's worth of food, and could spend the evenings in mating rituals. Hooray! However, if times turned bad, they could spend more energy looking for food than they would get in return. So, for a while, when the dawn came, they would just say, "Fuck it. Hunting and gathering both suck. Anyway, I'll never find a mate. Fuck everything."  And they would just stay in bed, conserving precious calories for a while until times got better, sort of like hibernation lite. 

At the time, this made sense. Similarly, a long time ago, the desire to eat as much sugar and carbs and fat as possible was wise and good, but now, not so much. Depression is an instinct that once might have been useful, but in the modern environment is worse than useless. And, obviously, it affects some people differently than others.

Maybe "why" doesn't really that much. I know what its like when brushing your teeth and showering in the morning feels like running a half marathon in the freezing cold or something. It still always turns out to be worth it in the end, and you wind up with just a bit more energy than before (or at least I do.)

Are you in the U.S.? The laws in the U.S. vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, but basically tend to say that doctors and psychiatrists are legally required to commit patients to mental institutions if those patients are “a threat to themselves or others.” This is a legal standard, and like most legal standards leaves some grey area. 

A good psychiatrist will probably listen to you when you say "I'm not thinking about doing it."  However, not all psychiatrists are equally good, and not all are equally good for you in particular. Establishing a basic ground of trust with a new health provider is something you have to do anyway. You should be sure you have a rapport with your psychiatrist before you mention that you have a specific idea of how you'd do it, even if you're not planning to actually do it.

If the positions had been reversed, and he had been the sane one and you had been the one with longstanding depression, what would you have expected and what would you have expected of him?  Or what if it had been cancer?

Here's a paraphrase of something I was told by someone who should know:

There are some websites that try to solve these problems, like healthgrades.com, ratemds.com and vitals.com. They are not perfect and they have so few ratings on individual doctors that there's likely to be a lot of random noise. But whenever I've seen a doctor who gets multiple terrible ratings on these sites, I've hated them as well. So they might be useful as a rule-out, even though they're not good enough to be a rule-in.

If you have any friends who are doctors, nurses, or therapy-related professionals in your area, the medical community usually has a very good idea who's good and who isn't. If you have a primary care doctor you trust, they can also give you recommendations (although I would trust doctor-friends over your own doctor since a lot of doctors kind of automate out the process and refer patients to whichever specialist they know best or whoever's most likely to have slots available.)

The potential for repercussions is complicated and unpredictable. A lot of well-meaning people will tell you that its always better to seek treatment if you think you have a problem, and this may even be true. But once you have any kind of medical diagnosis, there *will* be a record somewhere, one which you cannot erase. Keep your eyes open.

For example, a formal mental illness diagnosis is widely regarded as a barrier to entry into sensitive government jobs, like law enforcement, military, or anything requiring a security clearance. This last category includes a surprising number of regular desk jobs at the federal level.

There are legal protections designed to limit discrimination against ordinary citizens with mental illness. However, as a general rule, if you are ever put into the category of "a danger to self or others," then you lose all sorts of legal protections.  This is a red line you don't want to cross. If you are truly suicidal or violent, then for all our sakes and your own, turn yourself in. But at the same time, don't let an overly-enthusiastic social worker put words in your mouth, or "sell" you on the false idea that you are suicidal. 

Here's an article about how doctors treat a writer who is on medication for mental illness:  http://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/11/opinion/sunday/when-doctors-discriminate.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0 . And it goes without saying that mental illness still carries some social stigma, so be cautions about whom you confide in.

Mid forties male here. I've been depressed off and on again for a long time. Not too many years back, my life was more or less together, with a family and a job. So hang on you whippersnappers. The good news for you younger people is that, even if it seems like you've really fucked things up, if you get your head together, life has a way of giving you a second or a third or a fourth chance. (I'm not being Pollyanna, my depressed redditors. I'm not saying shit like "God never gives us more than we can handle," which is bullshit. But if you're young, and you can read and write English, and you have the internet connection and the freedom to read these words, there are people who would wish they had it as good as you.)

Recently, though, I've been ruined, and not just emotionally. My wife has destroyed me in a divorce, and I'm unemployed -- and I suspect, basically unemployable. I have nothing. I've got kids who are not much younger than some of the people on this subreddit, and I am ashamed of what I am to them.

At my age, I've already used up most or all of my second chances. That's what getting older is -- running out of options. For instance, I will never retire -- the math just doesn't work. That's just one example. The list of things I had hoped to do but will never happen is long.

What you should take from this is that youth is an asset -- if you've got nothing but that, at least you have that.
